Mr. HANCE J. LOGAN (Cumberland) presented the first report of the committee on Public Accounts as follows:
Your committee recommend that the quorum of this committee be reduced from twenty-one to eleven.
He said: I 'beg to move:
That the first report of the select standing committee on Public Accounts be concurred in.
What is the effect of this report?

The report has already been read. The effect is to reduce the quorum from twenty-one to eleven. The difficulty of securing a quorum in committees of this House has become almost a scandal. Last year we called this committee four times in succession, but were not able to secure the quorum of twenty-one. This year we have had the same experience, and this morning we h-ad to wait nearly an hour to secure a quorum. We were able to secure it only after sending to all parts of the building and trying to get members out of other committees. In order to carry on the work of this committee, it has been found necessary to have the quorum reduced, and I think eleven will be quite sufficient.
Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Fort William and Rainy River):
subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have listened with a great
deal of interest to the discussion which has thus far taken place on the budget, and while I do not intend to review the debate, I should like to take a few moments to deal very briefly with some of the remarks made by speakers who have preceded me.
The hon. member for Lunenburg (.Mr. Duff) made, I thought, a rather severe attack upon the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail), due to the fact that she had gone down to Cape Breton and investigated the conditions there in What I thought was a spirit of humanity. I do not think that the hon. member for Lunenburg did himself quite justice, and I do not think he did quite justice to the hon. member for Southeast Grey, in the rather severe attack which he made upon her last night. It is true of course that in this country, as in every other country there are people who are poor. Two thousand years ago the greatest teacher, the world has ever had said:	" The poor ye have always with
you," and unfortunately it is a blot upon our so-called civilization that this condition exists to-day very much to the same extent as it existed two thousand years ago. At the same time, looking at the question down there from the standpoint of the ordinary observer, or the standpoint of the ordinary reader of the newspapers-or, indeed, the ordinary reader of the debates of this House-and without in any way desiring to take part in the controversy, I do believe that conditions are anything but desirable, and I feel that the sympathy of' this House goes out to that section of the country which seems to be labouring under very depressing conditions to say the least. I will go further and say that it would appear to me that it might be wise on the part of this government to make a more thorough investigation than has yet been made of these conditions, with a view to seeing if we should not perhaps give such help to the people in that section of the country in their afflictions 
as we might give, under difficult circumstances, to the people of such a country as Japan or perhaps the Fiji Islands, if an earthquake or other disaster had come upon them.
My hon. friend from Lunenburg made a remark in regard to the tariff with which I have no quarrel, in which he praised the government for putting a tariff on slack coal. He said-and he will correct me if I am wrong- that he was a low-tariff man, but he complimented them on the fact that they had raised the tariff on slack coal. My hon. friend from Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) in his speech, telling that fish story from British Columbia, which takes at least three hours, has on other occasions taken, I think, very much the same attitude as my hon. friend from Lunenburg. He states that he is also a low-tariff man, but when it comes down to tariff protection on certain products which come from his constituency, he believes in a tariff.
Mr. DUFF; There is no coal in my constituency.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is coal in my hon. friend's province.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, in the province.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The .point that I am trying to make is that very often our cries for low tariff are more or less sectional. In other words, those who feel that they require a tariff for their own section of the country believe in a tariff, and I submit what I have already stated on other occasions^ that if wheat remained at the price it has been selling for the last two months, $1.50 or $1.75, as I hope it will, in order to give the people of the prairie provinces a just return for the labour and investment, we would hear very much less tariff discussion in this House and out of it than we have heard in the past, just as in the past few weeks we have heard very little tariff discussion from my hon. friends to my left.
The hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Argenteuil) a gentleman for whom we all have the utmost friendship, rose in this House as a defender, perhaps I should also say a pretender, regarding the budget we have been discussing. The hon. minister, with that kindly, honest, frank face, fairly oozes respectability, and I have noticed the more disreputable a case the government has to put forward the more sure they are to call upon my honest-appearing friend to oome forth and defend it. As I listened to him defending so eloquently-which he certainly did in a very able manner-the budget which has been presented, it made me think of an incident which

The Budget-Mr. Manion
occurred in the life of Sir John A. Macdonald. He had in his cabinet the Hon. John Oarling, who had a face almost as honest as that of the Minister of the Interior, and one day, after some particular action of Hon. John Carling, Sir John A. Macdonald studied his face for some little time and said to one of his friends, or I think it was to Hon. John Carling himself, "I have come to the conclusion that the good Lord never made a man as honest as you look." As I listened to my good friend the Minister of the Interior defending this farcical budget the other day,
I felt the House might well come to the same conclusion regarding him.
He also spoke of what he believes on the tariff question. He did not listen to the chimes he rang last year, but he did say that he believed in a lower tariff; in fact he believed in a tariff for revenue only. I think I am not misquoting him when I say that. The expression "tariff for revenue only" is used to my mind in a false sense, because a tariff for revenue only is a free trade tariff. There is no such thing as a "tariff for revenue only" being a protective tariff. England has a tariff for revenue only by which she brings into the coffers of her finance department something like $600,000,000 per annum on commodities which she does not produce in her own domain; in other words, five-sixths of the money brought into the coffers of England by tariff duties are raised upon sugar, tea and tobacco, three substances which England does not produce within her own shores. So that is a tariff for revenue only, and if Canada had a tariff for revenue only she would have free trade, because so long as you put on a tariff which protects at all you are putting on a protective tariff to the extent that it protects.
I wish to touch one other remark of the hon. Minister of the Interior, and then I shall proceed with my discussion of the budget. The hon. minister pointed out-and drew my attention to it at the moment-that Sir Henry Thornton had made a statement that in Northern Ontario a number of new industries had started up recently employing a lot of men. I venture to say that, without knowing the facts, that most of those industries are pulp and paper industries, not affected by the tariff at all. But at any rate I wish to point out particularly to my hon. friend that the day after he made his speech I noticed in the morning papers of this city an article stating that there was a disturbance in Sudbury, due to the many unemployed starting a parade of their own.
Dealing with the budget from the standpoint of the ordinary observer, I submit that this budget, in which there is a complete absence of any remedies for our present discontents, is like a train of fifteen cars carrying one passenger. It is a sort of peculiar political salad, made up of a strange compound of unconscious humour, misstatements of fact, homeopathic doses of both free trade and protection, and an oily dressing of hopes of better times to come. As to misstatements of fact, I need only draw the attention of the House to the statement in regard to the prosperous conditions prevailing in the Dominion, and more particularly and more emphatically to that fable of a surplus-that fable which my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) is talking about ad nauseam, but which should be classed among Aesop's fables.
I intend to deal very briefly with my conception of the so-called surplus which the Acting Minister of Finance has described. My hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) has dealt with it from the standpoint of an ex-Minister of Finance, my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) has dealt with it from the standpoint of a chartered accountant, but I intend to deal with it just from the standpoint of the man in the street reading the budget speech a number of times and trying to figure out where the Acting Minister of Finance gets his surplus. My hon. friend the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) has pointed out that in his view instead of hava surplus of 82,000,000 there is actually a deficit of about $100,000,000, and I venture to assert that he is pretty accurate in his analysis. But I intend to deal with this surplus, not on the basis of any figures placed before the House by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) or any of his colleagues, but simply from the standpoint of the figures given by the Acting Minister of Finance himself. I find that on page 1469 of Hansard he estimated the revenue for the fiscal year, accurately enough for his purpose, at $344,000,000, as against an estimated expenditure of $342,000,000, leaving a surplus of $2,000,000. I am giving round figures. Well, Sir, if you look back at the preceding page you will find that the Acting Minister of Finance gives the accounts for the railways and shows loans by way of cash charged to the net debt of the Dominion at something over $18,000,000, and loans by way of government bond issues of $46,000,000, which added together amount to $64,000,000. This converts his surplus of $2,000,000 into a deficit, according to his own figures, of $62,000,000.

The Budget-Mr. Manion

That we should charge this railway expenditure not only to our debt but to the ordinary accounts is evident to anyone who would treat these accounts fairly. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) in his speech before the Canadian Club of Montreal recently, reported in one of the Montreal papers, said:
Our ordinary debt may have decreased in the past few years, but the ordinary debt is not the only one, we have in addition to that the railway debt. Consequently the gross debt of this country is not only the ordinary consolidated debt, but the railway debt, and if one rises then the whole debt is increased, and if one is lessened then the debt can be decreased.
I quote the hon. member because he is a follower of the government and a friend of the Acting Minister of Finance, and yet he agrees that these railway charges should be included in the ordinary debt of the country, and I believe that when we talk of a surplus we have to take into account this railway expenditure.

speechtext: Would the hon. member include in what affects a surplus or deficit the amounts advanced to the National Railways or borrowed by them on capital account?

Mr. Speaker, we do that
in regard to harbours, canals and other public expenditure on capital, and unless there is some hope of getting back any of the money in the near future, certainly it should be charged to the national debt, and against surplus because the country is responsible for it.

No matter what it is for.
In 1922-3 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) charged up $80,000,000 advanced to our railways to the national debt according to the Acting Minister of Finance.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman surely
distinguishes between adding to the national debt or adding to the surplus or the deficit?

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Certainly. But the Acting Minister of Finance does not even add the railway bond advances to the debt, and he claims a surplus when in reality there is no surplus at all; in fact there is a deficit of $62,000,000 according to his own figures, though the cash deficit is not so much as that. We are just as responsible to the people for those expenditures upon the National Railways as we are for any other expeditures by the government, particularly in view of the fact that at present no one can expect within any reasonable time in the future that that expenditure will be paid back by the National Railways. It would be very much the same, 
Mr. Speaker, as if a civil servant of the higher grade in this city, receiving, we will suppose, $10,000 a year, spends $9,000 himself, and his wife and children, for whom he is entirely responsible, have run current accounts for another $5,000, making a total expenditure for his household of $14,000. Would my hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) claim that that gentleman had a surplus at the end of the year?

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No. But the hon. gentleman says that the whole $14,000 was spent on living. He does not say that anything was spent on purchasing a house or anything of the kind that would be an actual asset.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I said that this gentleman himself had spent $9,000, and his wife and children had spent another $5,000, or had run accounts for that sum, for which he is absolutely responsible. Could they claim a surplus?

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will say what the $9,000 and the $5,000 were expended for I will give him an answer.

speechtext:
No matter what it was
spent for, it was spent or he became responsible for its payment, and he would not have any surplus that year. I know what my hon. friend has in his mind, that some of that expenditure might have been capital expenditure which would be an asset. All right, he is responsible for it anyway, and being responsible for it he would not have a surplus, especially if he could not dispose of the asset as in our railway case.
K Mr. EULER:	It might be a liability, but
it would not affect his surplus.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if a gentleman, such as I speak of, has spent or become liable for $14,000 as explained, and then claims that he had a surplus on his $10,000 income, he would be suspected of having delusions of grandeur. I remember reading of an old Greek general who had won a very costly victory saying: " Another such victory will ruin us." I think that if we have many more surpluses such as the surplus that the Acting Minister of Finance has described in his budget speech this country will be ruined. It was Talleyrand who said that language is given us to hide our thoughts. But in Canada budgets are given us to hide our deficits.
But, Sir, that is not the worst, because on page 1469, the Acting Minister of Finance deals with unpaid arrears of interest from Greece and Roumania, $4,000,000, which those countries have asked the Dominion to apply

17S5
The Budget-Mr. Manion
to the principal owing-and upon which perhaps in the future they intend to pay interest -and he actually adds that $4,000,000 of unpaid arrears to his so-called surplus of $2,000,000, and says he has a surplus of $6,000,000! I think if that statement were read to one of the mummies in the British Museum it would take off its dried wrappings and laugh. What kind of gold brick financing, what kind of political shell game is the Acting Minister of Finance trying to put over on the unsuspecting people of this country? Sir, if you take the old South Sea Bubble, the Home Bank fiasco, and Get-rich-quick Wallingford, and roll them all into one, you would have nothing akin to what my hon. friend has been attempting to tell the people of Canada. I do not think that Get-rich-quick Wallingford, that prince of crooks, even in his palmiest days, attempted to put over such a deal on the people with whom he came into contact. I well remember in my earliest days in the west purchasing stocks in some pretty slick mining projects, but those slick mining deals, Sir, were the highest and soundest kind of financing compared with that which is exemplified in the budget speech of this year.
But that is not all. The Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on page 1470 of Hansard, says, referring to the $4,000,000 of unpaid interest due from Greece and Roumania:
This amount is available to be applied on account of our loans to the Canadian National Railways of $18,027,000, to Canadian Government Merchant Marine-
And so on. Well, sir, I think the Acting Minister of Finance has given us a splendid example of unconscious humour in that statement. There is still another delightful touch on page 1472, where, after telling us that he has quadrupled the duty on slack coal, he says that this change will remove the difficulties in the administration of the act. If he had said, remove the difficulties in multiplication instead of in administration, perhaps he would 'be nearer the truth, because he has increased the duties, I understand, from fourteen cents to fifty cents. I do not see how a difference in multiplication can make any difference in the administration of the act. Now that the famous Dennistoun case is off the boards, Mr. Speaker, I am going to keep this budget speech for light reading on dull days.
But, Sir, to speak seriously, should we not have the truth in regard to matters of this kind? Should the people of this country be treated like so many children? Should they not be told the facts with regard to their 114i
own financing? Should they not know the conditions which really obtain in Canada? Or are we to have a conspiracy of silence, or perhaps what is worse, a tissue of half truths, in dealing with the financial condition of our country? I am reminded of a remark made by Napoleon when he was referring to a German diplomat: He said, "That man. lies, too much. It is necessary to lie sometimes, but not all the time."
Sir, if you 'look back over the history of the ages that have gone you will find that many empires have risen, then have declined and fallen, particularly during the fifteenth, sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. That i3 exemplified by what happened in the case of Spain and Portugal; I mention merely these two for the purposes of the illustration. What was the cause of the decline and fall of these empires which had become very outstanding not only in commercial development and in industry but also in colonial expansion? They declined and fell because they were oppressed with unfair taxation and because they were oppressed with bad government. This Dominion of Canada to-day is to my mind suffering from exactly the same conditions. No one needs to elaborate the argument with regard to high taxation, because I believe that the taxation in Canada to-day is as high at least as the taxation was in 'any of those countries of which I speak; and so far as the bad government is concerned, that is manifested on every side.
Yet the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the Speech from the Throne made the statement that the only problem or the outstanding prohlem before the people today, was the cost of living. He apparently sees no problem to be solved in connection with the affairs of this country except the high cost of living. In view of that fact I made it my business to inquire of the Bureau of Statistics as to the cost of living in the past year, and I am going to show how the Prime Minister and his government are solving this problem. The Bureau of Statistics state that the index figures for each month with respect to foods, fuel, 'lighting and rent from last May to the present time were as follows:	May, 144; June, 144.2; July, 144.S;
August, 146.7; September, 147.2; October, 147.4; November, 148.4; December, 149; January, 150.3; February, 151.1. Well, Sir, as far as I can see, the problem of the cost of living is being solved by this government in exactly the same way as they are solving every other problem they have had to deal with, and that is by making it worse. All
17S6
The Budget-Mr. Manion

the conditions of this country have been getting worse and worse year by year since this government came into power.
What are the real problems of the country to-day, and what is the real solution of those problems? To my mind they are four, chiefly:	First, we must bring about a condition of less taxation by a proper and economical handling of our affairs. Secondly, we must have a stable tariff policy, providing for a tariff high enough to permit all our industries to continue. Thirdly, we must have an efficient immigration policy, and fourthly, we must have a wise railway policy. I am going to deal with the last two first, that is, the * immigration policy and the railway policy.
So far as an efficient immigration policy is concerned, there is no doubt that we need agriculturists in this country to populate and cultivate those millions of acres of fertile land which we have from the Atlantic to the Pacific. But I should like to draw the attention of the government to the fact that we have in various sections of this country besides the prairie provinces millions of acres of land to be developed. There are millions of acres in the Maritime provinces, in Quebec, in northern Ontario and in British Columbia. Take the section of country whence I come, northern Ontario; we have a country there as extensive in area as the British Isles and the German Empire put together, but while they have in the two European countries I have mentioned about a hundred million people, we have in northern Ontario from North Bay to the Manitoba boundary only about a hundred and fifty thousand. We have resources of all kinds; millions of acres of fertile land; we have hundreds of millions of tons of iron ore which some day will make that a great iron producing country. But that section to-day forms a gap between the east and the west, and the government might-well spend some cf its time populating that country to make traffic for the railways and to bridge that gap between the east and the west instead of sending out to the prairie provinces all the immigrants that come to our shores. At the same time, it is to be remembered that prosperity in our country will in itself bring immigrants here. In 1914, the year before the war, 400,000 immigrants came to Canada-a goodly number indeed; so that the conditions which it is often stated are not brought about by protection were actually being brought about in those years. Before the war we were getting immigrants as rapidly as we could absorb

them. At the same time, we all know that we have no room in the cities for more industrial workers, so that we should at least get our industries back into good condition before we permit immigrants to come to the cities and towns.	.

speechtext:
Oh, I do not suppose
there is any slavery system in this country which will keep anybody anywhere that he does not want to stay. But the fact is that we are not keeping our people in the country at all just now; they are going to the United States.
With regard to the matter of railway policy, we have in this country to-day three transcontinental railways where two would have been ample. We have railways sufficient at least for three or four million more people than we have. In other words, we are overbuilt in the matter of railways. What we need is increased population in a fairly prosperous condition. In other words, we need stability in business; we need work ,and [DOT]wages for our people; we need prosperity for the different sections of the country. Qne point that I would like to emphasize is this: we should have less spending by -our National Railways. The hon. ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) put a question on the order paper a few days ago and he received the reply that there was spent upon our National Railways during the past year, added to the new capital account, $118,000,000. That is a vast amount of money, Mr. Speaker, to add to our national accounts, to our national debts, in a sense-national obligations is the better word-in one year. I was thinking over the matter and I made it my business just this morning to look up the Public Accounts. What did I find? In 1900 our whole income, the entire revenue of this country, was only
151,000,000. I take this from ithe Public Accounts for 1924, page 47. In other words, in 1900 we were taking in less than fifty per cent of the amount which has been added to the account of the National Railways this year. The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) looks surprised, and so was

The Budget-Mr. Manion
I surprised when I looked that figure up. But I am going to give some other figures. In 1905 that amount had gone uip to $71,000,000 odd; in 1910, it had gone up to $101,000,000. In other words, our total receipts in 1910 were $17,000,000 less than was added to the national debt by the railways in the past year. It was not till 1912, just thirteen years ago, that this country took in receipts from all sources equal to the expenditure for the National railways during the past year. That appears to me a very serious state of affairs, and I think the government might well consider whether there is not some way of lessening such vast expenditures of the people's money as have been going on for the National railways during the past year.

Now I *itend to deal with the question of economy, because, Sir, so far as I can see, m3' good friend the Minister of Justice has no more conception than any other minister in this government of the need of economy in this country-certainly not if we are to judge by the expenditures which are going on under this government. I am going to prove that also by the budget speech of my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance. I think I can do it from memory. The Minister of Finance said in his budget speech that the decreased revenue in Canada in the past year was $52,009,000. He said that the decreased expenditure was $5,000,000, or a little less than 10 per cent of the decreased revenue. Now Sir, I wish to point out that private corporations would try to approximate those figures a little more closely than this government has approximated them. In the past year the Canadian Pacific Railway, which no matter what we may think of it as a company, and no matter what we may think of its rates, certainly deserves the respect of the people of this country for the manner in which it does its business, according to their annual report, which I have in my hand, had for the fiscal year ending December 31st last, gross earnings which were $13,334,000 less than the previous 37ear; but their working expenses were $13,083,000 less than the previous year. In other words, while the government in charge of the affairs of this country have decreased their expenditure by
The Budget-Mr. Manion

10 .per cent of tlieir decreased revenue, the Canadian Pacific Railway have decreased their expenditure by about, 96 or 97 per cent of their decreased revenue.

speechtext:
Maj"- I ask a question; merely for information? My hon. friend made the statement that there had been spent on fresh capital commitments on the National railways for the last year $118,000,000. Can he give me the exact statement?
Mr. MANIONNo, because I have not got the railway statement.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The figures I am giving are the figures given by the Minister of Railways to the ex-Minister of Finance, and will be found in Hansard of 16th March, page 1151. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that that $52,000,000 of decreased revenue, which has been .claimed by the Liberals as decreased taxation, is simply and plainly a proof of the business depression in this country; it is simply a proof of the fact that the4 people of Canada are not in a position to buy the things they used to buy in t'he past; they are not in a position, for example, to import the luxuries they used to import, and on which they had to pay duty. In my own city of Fort William, there are a number of closed-down plants, and the closing down of at least one or two of them is due to the lack of tariff protection. These plants have certainly not the expenses they had a year ago, but they have no income whatever. If this ministry goes on and brings Canada to the stage where she has no income whatever, where she is in bankruptcy, you will have no income, and then I suppose we shall have reached the stage of perfection because there will be nothing collected in taxes. This government goes gaily on spending on everything that comes to its mind, and cutting down expenses on practically nothing. It would be a hilarious farce if it were not for the fact that it is a tragedy to the people of Canada,. Here we have unnecessary expenditure going on on public works, unnecessary general expenditure of all kinds, unnecessary expenditures on the railways such as I have mentioned, unnecessary expenditures on royal commissions. I asked this government over a month ago for a list of the royal commissions that they had appointed since they came into power, and the expenditure on those commissions. Apparently they have been unable to figure up the expenditure yet, be-

cause I have not yet received my reply. I did, however, receive a reply as to two of these royal commissions this government have appointed, the pulpwood commission and the grain commission. The pulpwood commission cost $75,000 to the people of Canada, and the grain commission cost the people of this country $170,000. In other words, these two commissions, which gave their reports, have cost the people of Canada a quarter of a million dollars. So what must have been the cost for all the other royal commissions that have been appointed by this government? I venture to assert that there has been a cost of probably well over a million dollars, if not a million and a half, spent on royal commissions appointed by this government since they came into power, and appointed, as an hon. gentleman remarks, to save the government from the responsibility of deciding questions for themselves. As a consequence, we have high taxes and high expenditure in eveiy line of government. We have an income tax four or five times the income tax in the United States in almost every income range, and as a consequence we have this country being pushed fairly rapidly into the arms of the United States. And yet the Prime Minister insists that conditions in Canada are good and getting better, whereas in reality the conditions in Canada are bad and getting worse. It reminds me of a remark made by Lord Rosebery in that very charming story of Napoleon which he told in which he said that "at times it was difficult to know when Napoleon was deluding himself, when he was trying to delude others, and when he was simply talking at random for talking's sake." I think, Sir, the same remark might well be applied to the Prime Minister in his reference to the conditions in this country at the present time.

It is said that Nero fiddled while Rome burnt-

speechtext:
dreary scene and you are forever floored, as I am! That applies as much to this Dominion as to each individual in the country; because unless attention is paid to that philosophy this country cannot make the progress which it should make. I do not wish to go further into the question of economy because it requires no elaboration. The only people in Canada who do not seem to know that economy is needed, the only people in Canada who are paying no attention to the extravagance of the government, are the members of the government themselves.
Now, Sir, I must deal for a few moments with the question of a stable tariff policy for this country,-this will appeal to my hon. friend the member for Brome (Mr. McMas-ter)-a stable tariff policy for this country high enough to permit all our industries to continue, a policy which will give us not only confidence in our business but work for our unemployed, and give an opportunity for our Canadian boys and girls to remain in Canada and not be forced to expatriate themselves to the most highly protected country in the world to earn a living, and which will give, as well, an opportunity for tens, yes hundreds, of thousands of people from the crowded European countries to come over here and help us to develop this magnificent country which we possess. A proper policy of this kind will give our artisans the choice of employment instead of, as now, the choice of crossing to the United States or going hungry. What we want is to have our Canadian factories going, not to have, as is the case at the present time, foreign factories going whilst ours are idle, Canadian artisans idle while foreign artisans are busy. I wish to show here just in reply to one of the speakers who preceded me-I think it was the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean)-who claimed that conditions in the city of Brantford were in excellent shape, that the reverse is the case. I have here a list of names of those who in the past year have sent to this government protests against this cutting down of the tariff, and at the head of them is the council of the city 0f Brantford. I have on this list also Hamilton, Kitchener. London, Galt, Glen 'Williams, Peterborough, Woodstock, Paris. Carleton Place, St. Catharines, Montreal. Toronto and Tillsonburg. These are simply names that I happened to have under my hand; I know there must be many more. In addition to that I have seen protests from coal producers, the boot and shoe producers, the starch and syrup manufacturers, the iron pipe p.^ducers, the textile industry, the fruit growers, east and west, the steel 
producers, and the poultry producers. From all over this country we have had demands for tariff stability, for a tariff high enough to permit our industries to continue. And after all, Mr. Speaker, who has profited in the past year or two by the cuts in the tariff which this government has made?

The Budget-Mr. Manion
the business men in this country profited? I have made it my business, in every section into which I have gone, to ask every class of business men how business is, and never before in my life have I heard so many stories of business depression as at the present time. The whole country is depressed to-day.
It is not cheap goods that we get by a low tariff that we want in Canada; it is work and wages for our people.
I admit with Sir Arthur Currie, the general who made such a good reputation overseas, that perhaps we should talk a good deal of optimism, of patriotism in Canada. I have no criticism to offer to that. I talk it sometimes myself, but at the same time it is very difficult to be optimistic, patriotic, when you have no work and no food in the house. When unemployment and hunger come in at the door, patriotism and optimism fly out of the window, and that is why our people are flying across the border into the United States at this time. If we have prosperity in Canada, we shall have happiness in Canada; and if we have happiness in Canada, we, shall hold our people in this Dominion. The reason we have not prosperity, have not happiness in Canada-

The reason that we have depression and instability in Canada is because of the unstable attitude of this government on the tariff question. We do not need to go back beyond the last three years. We do not need to go back to the Liberal platform of 1919. All we need to do is to go back to 1922 when the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) brought in his budget at that time and said:	The tariff is low
enough; we are not going to have any more cuts; we have to have stability in the tariff if we are going to have stability in business in this country. Could anybody under those circumstances understand what this government really thinks on tariff questions? Is it possible that we can have stability in the countrj- at the present time? A consistent application of a weak policy would be far better than alternate applications of two opposing policies, the application of either one of which may be excellent in itself, but the application of both of which together can lead to nothing but instability as we have it in Canada to-day.

speechtext: My hon. friends do not applaud so heartily as they did a year ago. I notice, by the way, that no applause came from the other side of the House. subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Except for coal. It is only fair that it should be remembered that, in the Dominion of Canada to-day, Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia, those three provinces at least, are reasonably solid in favour of a tariff policy of protection.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I doubt that.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I submit they are. My hon. friend will have an opportunity to state his case later.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about some hon. members from Ontario in this section of the House?

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Some of the free traders from Ontario will not be here after the next election. I wras going to say that those provinces contain about 7,000,000 of the people of this country, which is a fairly good majority. I do not mean to say by that that I believe the prairie provinces or the Maritime provinces should have anything imposed upon them which would mean a loss to them, and I submit that the resolution of my right hon. leader, which was referred to in the discussion a few moments ago, shows that he realizes what we all realize to-day, that if the 7,000,000 people in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia are to have the tariff policy which they wish, and if the tariff policy is going to be a weight around the necks of the Maritime provinces or the prairie provinces, they must get some compensation from the 7,000,000 people.

anticipate that his right hon. leader would reimpose the duty on stumping machines?

CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is my hon. friend not
aware that in Germany material for shipbuilding is allowed in free?

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What has that to do with the matter? Does my hon. friend not admit that the British shipbuilders should protect themselves from being driven out of business by the Germans? And if labour is cheaper in Europe and the sta-dard of living lower, does he claim that we should adopt the same conditions in Canada, or should we protect ourselves against such a condition? The material is cheap also to the English shipbuilder. Why should the shipbuilder who has been carrying on so nobly for fifty or a hundred years permit himself to be driven out of business by German competition?
With regard to the politics of my hon. friend from St. James (Mr. Rinfret), I point out that Edmund Burke said that a political party consisted of a group of men banded together for the advancement of national progress by the promotion of some particular principle on which they were all agreed. What is the particular principle on which the Liberal party are all agreed? Is it the tariff? They have as many attitudes on the tariff as Heinz has of brands of pickles and sauces. We have the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) who is a free trader; we have the hon. member from Brome (Mr. McMaster) who is a free trader; and the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) who is a free trader-in the west; I do not know what he is in the east- and we have the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Argenteuil) who is a free trader, who has rung "the death knell of protection"-

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What is the hon.
gentleman's authority for saying I am a free trader anywhere?

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is the hon. minister a protectionist?

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, not in the

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I thought my hon. friend *would straddle the fence, if I put him to the test. These are a few of the Liberal free traders in the House. My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture disowns the free trade policy, so I will accept it that he is a protectionist.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes. But what will happen to the shipbuilders in England who are out of work and going hungry?

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is not industry in Canada
suffering to-day because of an unduly heavy overhead?

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, it is because of the instability brought about by the many attitudes assumed by the government in regard to protection.
I was speaking of the free traders on the other side of the house. I will mention the protectionists. I will put the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) among them if he wishes to go in. Then I will take the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) and the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) and my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs). These are a few of the protectionists in the House. I should not overlook my good friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), he is something of a protectionist, and I have often wondered why he did not become contaminated by the hon. member from Brome (Mr. McMaster) who is so extreme in his views. I could name a number of others, but I will not do so.
In regard to those on the other side of the House who have no policy at all, I will mention the Prime Minister himself, (Mr. Mackenzie King), because I venture to assert that not even the Prime Minister himself knows what policy he supports on the tariff question.
Is it on the Senate that they are agreed? I do not think so, because we have seen a speech by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) which does not agree with the attitude of the Prime Minister as expressed in his speeches in the western provinces. With regard to the railway question they are not
The Budget-Mr. Manion

all agreed, because sitting over here to my left is the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) an out-and-out protectionist and just two seats away from him we find my hon. friend from Laprairie and Napierville' (Mr. Lanctot), who wishes to give the National railways away for one dollar.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have always held the
same opinion on that subject.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I laid the trap for my
hon. friend and I knew he would say that.

speechtext:
My hon. friend said that I

speechtext:
I meant that my hon.
friend was in favour of national ownership. And my hon. friend beside him believes in giving away the National railways altogether.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We would be better off
in five years from now if we gave it away.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not intend to go into that question.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will tell the House what I think of my hon. friend and his party later. They are to blame for the railway situation.

speechtext: I do not know what abuse my hon. friend is uttering now, because there is too much noise.

what I do believe about my hon. friend and his friends.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hope it will be printable. My hon. friend says that this railway condition is due to us. Well, I am just going to see whether it is due to us or not. Perhaps I should be classed among those to whom it is due, but I do not think this party is responsible. In 1896 there was only one transcontinental railway in Canada. In 1904 Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his government started the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific, and before he went out of power in 1911 his government guaranteed
835,000,000 for the extension of the Canadian Northern railway from Port Arthur to Montreal, which made the third transcontinental railway.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Did the Conservative
party oppose that scheme in the House in 1911?

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not know whether
they did or not.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, they did not.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But I do know that Sir
Wilfrid Laurier started the scheme of guaranteeing $35,000,000 to extend the Canadian Northern railway from Port Arthur to Montreal, and so made it the third transcontinental railway. The fact that we have three transcontinental railways should be laid at the door of the Liberal party, not at the door of the Conservative party.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
permit me:	A railway running from the
prairies to Montreal is not a transcontinental railway. That was the Canadian Northern railway position when Sir Wilfrid Laurier went out of power. The Conservative government of British Columbia-

speechtext:
Built the onlj
paying part.

speechtext: Under charter-

My hon. friend is afraie

speechtext:
I rose and asked the
privilege of making a correction, which my hon. friend (Mr. Manion) gave me. The Conservative government following the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier through, 1 think, consultation with Sir Richard McBride, had the latter government issue a provincial charter to the Canadian Northern to build a line through the mountains to the coast. That started the downfall of the McBride government, and left-

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt my hon. friend but-

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Just another minute and
I will be through. I was trying to point out that my hon. friend was wrong in saying the Liberal party ever established a third transcontinental line. The Liberal government refused absolutely to aid the Canadian Northern extension into British Columbia, but-

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Sir Wilfrid Laurier granted the charter and declared there would be a third transcontinental. He himself is on record in Hansard as saying that he thought a third transcontinental railway was necessary. I will produce Hansard containing his speech in a few minutes.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, I
happened to be the minister to whom the Canadian Northern came for aid for the line

The Budget-Mr. Manion
through to Vancouver from the prairies, and Sir Wilfrid Laurier and myself absolutely refused that aid, saying they must make a success of their prairie line east, and after that the western extension might be considered. The Conservative party helped the Canadian Northern to build that extension, and thus are responsible for the third transcontinental line.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should
like to point out that while I am not going to argue about the part of the line in British Columbia, yet I do submit that the part of the Canadian Northern extending from the head of the lakes to Montreal, which was not needed at all, was started by the guarantee of $35,000,000 made by Sir Wilfrid Laurier before he w'ent out of power in 1911.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Did not my hon. friend
favour that?

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not know whether I favoured it at that time or not. I was not then handling the affairs of the country; my hon. friend and Sir Wilfrid Laurier were. In 1911 I was quite a young man-a good deal younger than my hon. friend, for which I presume he is a little sorry.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not a bit.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At the same time I submit that that line across northern Ontario where in 350,000 square miles there are only
150,000	people is part of the line which should never have been built under any circumstances. However, the hon. member for Laprairie and Napierville was getting rather bitter at my discussing railway matters-

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
By whom was that line
from Port Arthur to Montreal built, was it by the Liberals or by the Tories?

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not know who built
it, but the contracts were, let before the Liberal party went out of power.
But we have got some distance from the argument which I was making, Mr. Speaker. Burke once pointed out the need for some cooperation in regard to one principle for a party to be a political party, and I was showing that in railway matters, tariff matters and Senate matters the Liberal party have no unity of any kind; in fact, in all lines of thought they seem to be dwelling in a thick fog of confused ideas; but no, there is one principle as to which I should have made an exception: they are in agreement on the principle of power at any price-even the price of Canada. It was Daniel O'Connell who said that he could drive a coach and
four through any act of parliament. Well, Sir, you could march a whole battalion of soldiers through the principles of the Liberal party to-day without disturbing their ranks in any way.
Now, Sir, what does the Conservative party offer the country in place of the policies which I have been criticizing? They offer a stable tariff policy which will bring about prosperity and success; and they offer it to all classes, to manufacturers and to farmers-to the 2,000,000 farmers of Ontario and Quebec who require protection. These farmers require the home markets which surround their farms, the home markets of Montreal, Sherbrooke, Three Rivers, the home markets of Hamilton, Toronto, Brockville, Peterborough and other cities; and they require more protection than they are getting at the present time to keep out the millions of dollars' worth of farm products which are now being imported and which can be produced in Canada. I have under my hand a report from the Department of Trade and Commerce showing, at page 1420, the imports of farm produce, and fortunately it divides these imports into those that can be produced in Canada and those which cannot. The report shows that of fruits, vegetables and animal products which can be produced in Canada, there were imported in the year ending March 31, 1924, $149,201,000 -practically $150,000,000 worth of farm products, all of which could be produced here if we cared to produce them. We collected upon the products imported less than $29,000,000 in tariff duties, or something like 18 per cent; whereas our farm products going into the United States are charged at the rate of from 25 to 30 per cent. Let me give a few of the items. I regret that I am taking so much time,-	-

Could my hon. friend-
I am not going to make a speech this time- give the origin, say, of the butter and cheese that was imported? Perhaps he has not the figures-

speechtext:

time either, but I would like to understand why we were importing hides. Some hon. members in that part of the House stated in speeches that very few hides had been manufactured in Canada; that there was no market for hides because there was no manufacturing.

speechtext:
These are the figures of
two years ago.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE

two years ago; and by the way, I could have made the figures look very much worse if I had quoted those of three yeags ago. speechtext:
I have the facts here,
from the Bureau of Statistics. If there is any mistake it is a mistake of the Bureau of Statistics. I was going to say-

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I made the statement on
the basis of information supplied by the Department of Trade and Commerce of this government. Sometimes I do believe this government; in this case I do. I expected that question and I am quite ready for it. I confess that when I read the figures I had the same doubt that my hon. friend apparently has. But the figures show that in addition to that $149,000,000 worth of products imported which could have been produced on the farms of this country, we imported $236,000,000 worth of other farm products-that includes cotton, by the way. In other wordis, we imported into Canada in that year, according to these figures, $385,000,000 worth of farm products of all kinds, of which practically S150,000,000 worth were goods which could be produced on the farms of this country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend how much of that import consisted of goods Which were in season in Canada at the time the import was made?

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The very fact that the Department of Trade and Commerce in their statistics show that these are goods which could be produced on the farms of Canada indicates that they came in at seasons when they could be produced here, otherwise they would not have been included in such statistics.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, no.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, suppose strawberries came in, as they do, a couple of weeks earlier from the southern states than they are produced in Canada, should we take away the taste for strawberries on the part of the people of Canada so that they will not buj Canadian strawberries when they come ini Take the Okanagan valley; in that section of the country the fruit growers are up against the competition of the producers of Washington, Oregon and California, whose products come into our country at least a couple of weeks earlier than the products of our Canadian fruit farmers appear on the Canadian market. Well, should we take away from the people of the prairie provinces, or the people of Canada generally, if you will, the taste for fruits, and permit our fruit farmers in the Okanagan to go out of business? I submit we should not.

The Budget-Mr. Manion
I was pointing out that the United States has had the most remarkable development of any country, bar none, in the history of the world. I was going to say that Mr. Blaine, who had a debate with Mr. Gladstone in 1S96 on free trade and protection, which we are still debating, pointed out that between 1812 and 1861 the United States had tried free trade three times, and that after each one of these trials there were depression, unemployment, and panics. He said also- and this is according to the facts-that from 1861 on, after they had adopted a consistent high-tariff policy in the United States, progress and prosperity had been practically unbroken in that country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Surely the hon. member, who is interesting us so much in his discourse, does not pretend that since 1861 they have not had panics, and severe panics, in the United States?

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Oh, no. I have said in this House before, and I repeat it now, that no policy that anyone has yet discovered is a panacea for all hard times. There will be hard times occasionally in every country. But I submit that the hard times which occurred in the United States after that later period to which I have referred were very small in comparison with the periods of depression that had prevailed before. And, what is further, the progress of the United States from 1861 to the present day has been the most remarkable in the history of the world. So I submit that we should be more ready to copy the policy of a country which we so much resemble, the United States, than the policy of two little islands in the North sea whose area is only one-thirtieth of ours and whose conditions are altogether different from ours. I submit that that is the method by which we may succeed.
I am going to take the liberty of again quoting President Coolidge. He points out, in the same inaugural address to which I have referred-and I am very near the end of my remarks:
These policies of better international understandings, greater economy and lower taxes have contributed largely to peaceful and prosperous industrial relations.
And he says:
Under the helpful influences of restrictive immigration and a protective tariff, employment is plentiful, the rate of pay is high and wage earners are in a state of contentment seldom before seen.
That, I think, is a just reply to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) when they said the other day that there were twenty million unemployed artisans in the United States.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the statement was not made by either of the gentlemen referred to. If my hon. friend will stick to the facts-

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will my hon. friend tell me who made it?

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The record will show who made it, and who was quoted as making it.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This is a piece of fancy quibbling, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Justice threw it at me across the floor of this House when I was speaking the other day, and then the Minister of Labour* came in and quoted the words. I know who made the statement; he quoted Mr. Green as saying it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, were they trying to put over a hoax on the people of this country? Were they just talking to hear themselves talk? Or were they really trying to confuse the people?

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, there was no hoax being attempted at all. It was merely a statement of what a prominent representative of labour in the United States had said-no more; no less.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, it is a rather extraordinary attitude for the Minister of Labour to take. speechtext:
Rather strangely, my hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) pointed out on the floor of this House just the other day how good conditions were in this country in 1920. Not only that, Mr. Speaker, but the exodus from Canada at that time was very little: industry was stable; and, more important, the nations of Europe had not then got back to normal production and normal competition. But since that time these conditions have all changed. We have now the exact reverse of what was taking place then. European competition has come back, so much so that they are dumping their goods of all classes into this country, and putting out of business all classes of industry here. What is perhaps more important, this government has come into power, with as many tariff policies as a centipede has feet. The United States has also raised its tariff. The tariffs of every nation of the world have been raised except the tariffs of England and Canada, the two countries that are suffering more from depression to-day than any other country in the world. As a consequence of these changed conditions, the bottom began to drop out of business, and has been dropping out ever since, and everybody knows it except the government.

Let us look at the basic conditions in the United States and Canada. The United States national debt is not much less per capita than is ours. Our trade per capita is greater than thehs. Our bank reserves are good, our railway development is good, our national wealth is great. And yet we are not prospering as they are over there. According to the words of President Coolidge-I choose to take his word in preference to that of the Minister of Labour-conditions are good over there, and everybody knows conditions are bad in this country. What are the reasons for the difference? The chief reasons are that taxation is high in this country, higher than it is in the United States-our income tax, for example, is much higher. Secondly, the tariff of the United States is about twice as high on practically all lines of goods as our tariff.
Einally, Sir, we need a cool head and a strong hand to handle the affairs of this country. Instead of that, we have a weak head, and a hand that cares for nothing except holding the sceptre of power.
I have read a good deal of history in my time, and I have found that there have been a number of weak governments, but I have never found any government, except one, that could equal this government in incompetence, and that was the government of the Sultan Abdul Hamid, in Turkey, in 1885. He ordered the killing of the Armenians. This government is not killing the Armenians; it is killing industry, and driving out of our land into exile in a foreign country our Canadian boys and girls. Not only is this government not killing the Armenians, it is actually helping the Armenians, and the Czecho-Slovakians, the Germans, the French, the British, the Americans-everybody but. Canadians. May I also point out that that famous Liberal, Mr. Gladstone, whom my good friend from La-prairie and Napierville (Mr. Lanctot) would not criticize, I presume, having in mind this government of Abdul Hamid made a famous speech in which he said the Turks should be "driven out of Europe bag and baggage." I say, Mr. Speaker, that the only salvation for this country is to drive this government bag and baggage from the Dominion of Canada, and to put in power a government that will bring into force a proper policy of economy, and a proper tariff policy which will give stability to industry, provide work for the unemployed, develop our resources, and build up a nation where our boys and girls can remain and find work instead of being forced to go to the United States to get it; a country where we will be able to look after hundreds of thousands of immigrants coming in from

The Budget-Mr. King (Kootenay)
the crowded countries of Europe. We must not only develop a spirit of love for our own country, but we must provide opportunities for our own boys and girls to indulge that spirit of love for their country. We must build up a proper protective policy which will bring about industrial development in this country, so that our boys on the farms and in our industrial centres will be able to remain in Canada and make a living at home.
About sixty years ago Macdonald, Cartier, Brown and the other Fathers of Confederation had the vision to dream of a great nation in Canada, extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific and from the Great Lakes to the Arctic ocean. If we are going to bring about a realization of that dream, we must profit by the lessons of history of the nations which have gone before.

My hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) will not say "hear, hear" to this, though it is just as true. The lessons of history teach me that there has been no country in the world that has ever progressed and reached prosperity except under a protective tariff. I make no exception when I say that. I do not wish to be diverted again, because I have taken up too much time now. But Great Britain, up till 1846, had the highest kind of protection, so high that she at times prohibited imports into Britain of lines of goods that interfered with home producers. She did not bring in free trade until 1865. For ten or fifteen years after 1846 Great Britain had duties on about four hundred lines of goods. It was not until Gladstone brought in his final free trade budget in 1S60 that they had free trade in England. Up to the time they had protection in England, and that is only sixty or seventy years ago, England was the most highly protected country in the world. She was protecting her industries of every kind, and she only brought in free trade when she had become the master of the world from the standpoint of industrial production, when she had become the workshop of the world, and hoped to remain so, because they thought then Cobden was correct when he said that if England adopted free trade, all the countries of the world would adopt it in the next ten years. I could argue this further with the hon. member for Brome. but I do not wish to take the time. I say, Mr. Speaker, that no country has ever become great industrially or commercially except under a tariff policy of protection. That tariff policy of protection is being fully employed by all the countries of the world 115
to-day except Canada and England. Not only is that a precept which we should live up to, but we should have a policy of economy. The United States and England are living up to that precept of economy, and consequently are cutting down their national debt, whereas in this country, taking the figures of the Acting Finance Minister himself, we have added $13,000,000 to our national debt in the past year.
Let us get into line with these different policies. Let us adopt the policy of lower taxation, by cutting down the expenditures of this government. Let us adopt the policy of protection, which will keep our home markets for our Canadian people, and permit them to compete with the other countries of the world. Let us adopt a policy of economy on the railways. Let us adopt a policy with an efficient immigration as its aim. Adopt these four as the corner stones in the building up of our nation, and cement them with a united Canadian spirit, and it appears to me you will then bring about that progress, prosperity and content which the people of Canada desire at the present time.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is surprising,
Mr. Speaker, where party exigencies will force our hon. friends opposite. They have been touring this country and in and out of parliament complaining that the people of Canada are exporting their excess production of raw material. The nation is very much like an individual who, to pay his debts and carry on, must sell in the markets open to him the products of his energy. I cannot think my hon. friends are really serious when they talk as they are talking these days of a tariff wall that would prevent the importation of any manufactured goods into Canada and of an embargo that would prevent the raw

materials of the country going out of Canada. If that is so, and if it should come to pass, then the Lord help the people of Canada. Conditions are bad enough to-day, and they were bad enough in 1914. Conditions were bad enough between 1878 and 1896. But if this policy that is being promoted and being announced by our hon. friends opposite- that is a high protective policy that will not permit importation of manufactured goods into Canada and an embargo on our raw materials-is to be adopted, then I am satisfied there will be no balanced budget, and Canada will not be in a very happy or prosperous condition. There is a lot of hectic talk these days about the export of our raw materials. To-day in every line of our basic industries we are producing more than we can consume. Is that production to cease or to be restricted to our own requirements? Surely not. As regards three of our basic industries, forestry, agriculture and fisheries, under proper scientific handling they can be conserved and be made increasingly valuable. In the case of forestry this is proven in Norway and Sweden, much older countries than ours, which to-day under a proper system of conservation of their forests are exporting their raw products and selling them in the markets of New York and Boston in competition with those of Canada and the United States.

What raw forest products
are coming from Sweden and Norway to the markets of New York and Boston? I mean absolutely raw products, such as saw logs?

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend
has asked me about raw products from Norway and Sweden entering the American markets, and I have given him what I understand to be one of those raw products. But who are our greatest competitors to-day in those markets in regard to newsprint and kraft paper? It is these little countries whose forests have been cut and recut for centuries, but through a proper system of conservation those forests to-day are producing in competition with the forest wealth of this great continent. There is no question that there has been frightful waste and extravagance in the handling of these great natural resources, but the waste and destruction has not been in the marketing of the raw products, it has been incident to the carelessness of our people. Fire has been the chief destructive cause. The homesteader in clearing his land has not taken the care he should have taken. The prospector exploring ore veins has at times found it convenient to remove the timber in order that he might 'better see the character of the country and its geological formation, and he has resorted to fire. But the homesteader and the prospector have not been the worst offenders. We know that railway companies in times past have not properly protected the forest growth adjoining their right of way. The lumberman himself has not always taken proper care to ensure his limit against fire. Many of those who are complaining most bitterly to-day against our raw products being exported are probably more responsible than any others for the terrible destruction of our forest wealth in the past. Fortunately to-day there is a more wholesome regard on the part of the people for our forest wealth; they are beginning to realize what an important part our forests play in the regulation of our rivers and streams, our climate, and so forth.
All our governments to-day, provincial as well as federal, have forestry departments whose staffs are composed of men who have graduated from forestry schools. They are devoting a great deal of time to the conservation and improvement of our timber resources, but they have hadi considerable difficulty in educating the people to the necessity of voting large expenditures for this work. Anyone who is familiar with lumbering operations on the Pacific coast, particularly on Vancouver island, knows that the lumber men in moving tremendous trees through any section of the country take off all the young, small growth with their drag line. This destroyed growth dries out and in a very little time becomes a fire hazard. As my hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie) said last night in his very interesting and instructive address, when this brushwood takes fire it throws out such a tremendous heat that the chances are that the seed bed will be destroyed and there will be no fresh growth of timber for many years to come. I have travelled through the inland portions of northern British Columbia, and have seen evidences of fires which probably occurred 100 to 150 years ago, and only in the last few years has nature begun to reforest. Fire is the greatest evil we have to contend with although it is true that in certain sections of the country trees suffer from other causes. For instance, recently in New Brunswick, there has been widespread destruction through the attacks of the spruce bud worm, whole sections of spruce having died and a few years later they will look as if they had been fireswept. But eventually science will entirely control these insect pests. The only agency, however, to prevent fire is proper regulation of timber operations, adequate protection and careful patrol work during the fire season,-all of which is going to cost money. In addition to taking these measures against fire, some of our provincial governments-most of the timber being under their control-are making surveys of such sectioas as are suitable for reforestation, and we find to-day that large areas are being set aside and protected to allow nature to reforest.
With respect to agriculture, we have only to look at the older countries of Europe to realize that our great competitors in Great Britain are Denmark, Belgium and Holland. We know that under scientific methods the products of our soil can be shipped to their ultimate market in the finished state to compete with those of any other country. This is also true with regard to our fisheries. The fishing industry by scientific treatment can be made ever-producing. I noticed within the last few days that a conference is being held in British Columbia between the United States and Canadian interests in order that a rehabilitation of the salmon fisheries on the Fraser river may take place. In line with that policy this parliament adopted two years ago a treaty with the United States government pertaining to the conservation of the halibut banks on the Pacific coast off Prinee Rupert. I personally am desirous that there
