The Budget-Mr. King (Kootenay)
shall be such a development in Canada as will result in the manufacture in our own country, as far as humanly possible, of our raw material into finished products. But to say that that must be done and that there should also be embargoes to prevent any material from going out in its raw state is absurd; it is a policy that would not be tolerated for a moment by the people of Canada.
We have a different condition in the mining industry. It is true that the ore that is taken out of the ground cannot be replaced by human intelligence or by scientific effort, but surely, having regard to the tremendous wealth we have in these mineral products, the extent of which is practically unknown to the Canadian people to-day and will not be fully known for many years, it is not the time to say to the people of Canada that they shall not ship out of the country the raw material from the mines. It is interesting to view the history of the parties in this regard. I may be mistaken but I have yet to learn of any act on the part of the Conservative party while they were in power, from 1911 to 1921 or in the period preceding, which tended toward the development of refining processes in connection with our ores in Canada. I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to contrast that policy, or lack of policy, on the part of our hon. friends with the policies enunciated and put into practice by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his government in the years they were in office. By a system of bounties the iron and steel industries in Canada have been built up. These industries have had their ups and downs, and we know that iron and steel are being made from our ores and that the products of this refinement are being used in the commerce of our country. The bounties as applied to the lead and zinc industry were a greater success. The history of that policy is rather interesting. At a time when the lead and zinc industry in British Columbia was apparently going out of business, the government undertook to set aside a certain sum of money to be used in the form of a bonus to be paid in accordance with the value of the ore refined. Before the period limiting the bonus had expired the stimulation to the industry had been such and the market conditions had been so improved that the price attained by the mineral was in excess of the price on the basis of which the government had agreed to pay the bonus, so that nothing more was required to be done so far as the bonus was concerned. To-day we have the lead and zinc industry well established in western Canada. Canada is making more lead 
and more zinc than she requires for her own needs, and is becoming an important factor on the world's market in connection with these products.
The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie) an evening or two ago, as I have stated, gave us a very interesting address on the subject of timber waste. But he hardly arrived at a conclusion. He came pretty nearly up to an embargo, but he went back to the question of waste; the hon. gentleman is too shrewd, too clever a business man to go that far. He said in conclusion that he was not satisfied that an embargo would be the proper thing; he thought perhaps an export duty might be wise. If I followed him correctly, I think that was what he said. Well, I do not take exception to my hon. friend's attitude. I am not sure that we have arrived at the position where we should impose export duties on raw material. The question is a debatable one, especially at this time when Canada's position is such that she must have revenues to meet the interest on her national debt, as well as to reduce the debt itself. There is a field there that might be surveyed by experts, bearing upon the question whether Canada would be entitled to take some revenue from the raw products by way of an export duty. I would be prepared to debate and consider that, but as to an embargo, I would say no.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have not refused, Mr. Speaker. I have declared my position, and have tried to make it clear to this House. I have stated that in times of stress conditions may arise which would make an embargo on certain products necessary. But as a policy for a great party in conjunction with a high tariff policy-well, the embargo is the limit.
Just before the opening of parliament this year, Mr. Speaker, we had a rather unusual display of activity on the part of our friends opposite in an attempt to precede His Excellency the Governor General in his annual speech to this House. In the Ottawa Journal a day or two before the meeting of parliament, the Conservative party, through their leader, stated the policy which they were prepared to follow; and that policy appeared in the news columns of the press of the country generally. This statement of policy reads very nicely; it would seem to be a panacea for all Canada's ills. In fact, it reads very much like a patent medicine advertisement. The right hon. leader of the opposition proposes a policy of increased protection, stating that it would give new life to Canadian industry, would enlarge the Canadian market for farm products, would create employment for our workers, increase traffic for our railways- by which alone, they state, an all-round reduction in freight rates can be secured. It would also add to the revenue, they say, thus permitting a reduction in internal taxation. Hon. gentlemen opposite would lead the people to believe that if Canada was touched
by this magic wand of protection all these things would come about. The proposals are so incredulous that one wonders if he is not living in fairyland.
There is nothing new in the policy of high protection. As far as the Canadian people are concerned we have had it in operation for a period of many years, and it is in operation to-day in some instances. I need take only one example, the automobile industry, which enjoys a protective tariff of 35 per cent. That duty may not be in accord with what our hon. friends opposite are going to propose when they get into power; that may be too low for them. I listened to the former Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) the other day when he was trying to convince this House that in view of the conditions in Canada we should adopt a protective policy similar to that adopted by the government of France. He read from the French tariff, showing that the schedules had been increased by 1,000,
2,000	and 3,000 per cent in some cases. I think we might fairly assume that for every $100 the manufacturer puts into an automobile, he has a protection of $35, and I think we may also fairly consider that at least adequate protection. Hon. gentlemen opposite say that if we gave protection of that character, we would! then turn into the pockets of our workmen the expenditure necessary to manufacture this necessary utility; tout has it worked out that way? I find that in the year 1920 we imported 13,079 cars, valued at $14,035,000; in 1923 we imported 7,987 cars, valued at $11,038,000; in 1924, we imported 10,889 cars, valued at $11,442,000; making the value of the total importations for the three years, $36,515,000. So this much vaunted protection has not worked in this case. The imports in those three years amounted to $36,-
515,000,	and if I were to follow the course of my hon. friend the former Minister of Finance, who took the importations of manufactured goods the other day, divided them by 1,200, and then said that that many thousands of people would have had employment in this country if we had had protection, I would take these figures: Dividing 36,515.000 by 1,200 gives 30.428. Divide that by three again, the imports covering three years, and you have 10,142 workmen that should have but did not have this expenditure in Canada on account of this high protection. The thing is a fallacy, Mr. Speaker. It does not work.
The automobile industry is, of course, an important one to Canada. I was rather amazed when I found the extent of the importations, but more greatly so when I looked at the ex-

The Budget-Mr. King (Kootenay)
portations from Canada. I find that in 1922 we exported $14,883,000 worth, in 1922, $8,082,000, in 1924, $37,742,000, or in those three years Canada exported automobiles to the value of $60,607,000. In addition to that, we exported in the same period $8,100,000 worth of automobile parts; so it is a rather important industry.
My hon. friends opposite might say-I would expect them to say, and I say it in order that they will not-look at the growth of this industry under high protection. They would say high protection had made it possible for Canadian manufacturers to export these automobiles. We know that is not so. Capital has come into the automobile business in Canada on account of certain preferences which the Canadian people enjoy in certain markets which the Americans do not enjoy, and that is why this development of the industry has taken place, and why there is this large export business.

speechtext:
I am satisfied
that hon. gentlemen opposite will have a very difficult task in trying to convince the people of Canada that a policy of high protection such as they advocate will be to the advantage and interest of the Canadian people. If this policy is of such great value, I am wondering, and I think the people of Canada are wondering, why in heaven's name did not the Conservative party bring this policy into effect in 1911? They cannot claim they did not do so then on account of the war, because from 1911 to 1914 they had a period of tranquility, and again from 1918 to 1921 they

had a further period. In 1911 the Conservative party, which to-day is proposing a high protective tariff, came into power on the defeat of the greatest trade agreement that was ever made by a Canadian government, an agreement which if it was in force to-day would mean prosperity to the Maritime provinces, prosperity to the provinces of central Canada, prosperity to the prairie provinces, and prosperity to the province of British Columbia. But not having this agreement, Canada has been forced to go further afield for her markets, and it can be said to the credit of her people that she has succeeded, and has not been daunted by the mistake she made in 191L The Canadian people have gone forward and steadily increased the growth of their export, so that to-day Canada stands per capita as the greatest exporting nation in the W'orld.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before six o'clock I had not only dealt with the criticism of the official opposition on the budget but I had also gone to the point where I think a government are entitled to go. That is, that when the party opposing have laid down their policy as a remedy for the conditions that exist, they should try and show the fallacies of that policy. My hon. friend the member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion), who has a very excellent vocabulary w'hich he does not ahvays use with discretion, made use of the term "gold brick." I propose to employ that same term now because it is absolutely applicable with respect to hon. gentlemen opposite. That party gold bricked the people of Canada in 1911. They are the very same men who to-day-through the press, and by their speeches on public platforms and in parliament-are libelling the government of this country and depreciating the efforts of our people. However, I do not think there is much danger of the people falling for those proposals coming from the source from which they do. "Once bitten twice shy," and the people of Canada have not forgotten 1911 and the years that followed.
Sir, I do not believe that any good will ever come to a party that decries its country. In the early days of this parliament it was said that the group of members to the left of the official opposition were pessimistic as to Canada's future. If that was so at

The Budget-Mr. King (Kootenay)
the beginning of this parliament as respects our Progressive friends, all I can say is they never reached the state of gloom and bitterness that prevails in the Conservative party to-day, a condition which is more characteristic of the leaders of the party than of the rank and file. The most notable examples, probably, are the right hon. leader of the opposition and his lieutenant from the city of Vancouver, one of the finest cities in Canada, a city that has enjoyed since 1922 a development unknown in any other seaport city in the world let alone in Canada. This development synchronizes with the new life that has struck western Canada.
My hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) was abroad last summer and since returning to Canada has been busily engaged in making public addresses. He has assumed an attitude that is rather surprising to members of this House, apparently being desirous of copying his friend and leader. Both gentlemen have developed into what might be termed common scolds. My hon. friend from Vancouver Centre is not satisfied to scold the people of Canada and the members of this House, but gushingly states that he told the people of the Old Country last year what he thought of them and their policies, and he adds "I was received with great response." My hon. friend mistook courtesy for response. Let me say that I do not believe it is the duty of any member of the Canadian parliament to go to Great Britain and tell the people there what they should do. I have sufficient confidence in the statesmen of Great Britain to leave Great Britain's problems to her own people to solve.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre in an address delivered since he returned from England has intimated to the people of Canada that the policy adopted by this government last session, whereby the government reduced the import duties on the instruments of production in the basic industries, had led to blue ruin in the province of British Columbia. He stated that some 350 or 400 men were thrown out of employment on account of the adjustment of the duties on logging equipment. I was rather surprised to hear that statement because I had been in western Canada last fall and met the men who are engaged in the manufacturing of this kind of machinery, and they did not tell me they were going out of business. Accordingly I thought I should ascertain the facts because my hon. friend has the faculty of speaking with some conviction. I made inquiries and I am now going to read to the House what the facts are in regard to that statement
I will read a telegram sent to me from Vancouver dated March 10, 1925:
Hon. J. H. King,
Minister of Public Works,
Ottawa, Ont.
I have been continuously in commercial engineering in Vancouver since 1902. I know every firm manufacturing or handling machinery in British Columbia. No concerns manufacturing logging equipment have gone out of business since the lowering of tariff. Present depression due to slackness in lumber industry. Only two concerns are engaged exclusively manufacturing logging equipment in this province, namely Empire Manufacturing Company and Tyee Machinery Company. Last named company also imports logging engines manufactured Portland, Oregon, and geared locomotives from Lima, Ohio. These two concerns have never employed more than fifty men in their combined operations. Undoubtedly lowering of tariff has been of great benefit to British Columbia especially coast, depending as it does on the lumber and logging industry and has done no injury to small manufacturing concerns located here. Am certain one large logging and lumbering concern would employ more men and distribute more in purchases and payroll than all concerns engaged exclusively in the manufacture of logging . equipment in the province. Statements made that any firms manufacturing logging machinery employing 250 to 300 men have gone out of business since tariff reduction last year absolutely without foundation.
George A. Walkem.
I know Mr. Walkem, but not intimately. I have met him. He is not a supporter of the Liberal party. He is a mechanical engineer, who has practised his profession in British Columbia since 1902, and who has been closely associated with engineering and particularly that form of engineering in the province. Last summer the people in his constituency saw fit to elect him to the local legislature of British Columbia.
My hon. friend also referred to and produced a petition from purported employees in the shoe manufacturing business in British Columbia. I want to assure my hon. friend and the petitioners that the government's tariff policy as regards British Columbia, that is, the lowering of duties on the instruments of production, will do more for the shoe business in Vancouver than his highly protective policy. But my hon. friend has seen fit to place his own interpretation on business conditions in British Columbia, and I think it is only fair that parliament should know the real state of affairs. I have in my hand a statement of the Financial Times of March 6, which reads:
Industrial progress in British Columbia shown by workmen's compensation figures from Canadian Bureau of Financial Times, Vancouver. Statistics compiled by the Workmen's Compensation Board of British Columbia are indicative of the industrial development of that province during the year 1924. According to the figures published, it is estimated that more than $160,000,000 was expended last year on payrolls in industries under the Workman's Compensation Act. For 1923, the payroll amounted to $153,548,944 as com-

The Budget-Mr. King (Kootenay)
pared with $128,592,502 in 1922. There was a corresponding increase in the number of industries established and operated, 1,550 new firms commencing business during 1924.
I first saw this statement in the Victoria Times and later in the Financial Times, and I have quoted the Financial Times because it cannot be said to be a party organ. I thought it well to confirm this newspaper statement, and I wrote to the chairman of the compensation board asking if the statement in the Times would be confirmed by his board. He writes me as follows:
The Hon. J. H. King,
Minister of Public Works,
Ottawa,
February 26, 1925.
Dear Doctor:
I am in receipt of your telegram reading as follows: "Would be glad if you would confirm statement made in Victoria Times, February, 14, regarding increased number of new firms doing business in the province in 1924 and increased payroll between 1922 and 1924."
I was unable to get a copy of the Victoria Times but . take it that the Times copies a report from the Vancouver papers. I accordingly wired you as follows: "There were 1,550 new firms commenced business in this province during last year. Payrolls of 1924 were at least $22,000,000 greater than 1922"
which I now beg to confirm. The reason I cannot give you the definite payroll figures for 1924 is that we have not yet audited all the employers' payrolls for 1924. There audits will not likely be completed before June or July of this year. However, we have assessed on the basis I have given you and in every single year our assessment has been found to be under the actual payroll; hence you can rest assured that the figures I have given are within the amount.
Conditions in British Columbia are better than they have been for the past four or five years. I have never known such a unanimous feeling of optimism as is now being displayed by the larger employers. Nothing in my opinion can hold British Columbia back from rapidly forging ahead.
I think the information compiled in our records gives more accurate indication of business conditions than any figures that can be compiled by others.
E. S. H. Winn.
Chairman.
The statements that my hon. friend has been making in his many addresses are statements that would lead the people of eastern Canada to believe that conditions in British Columbia are not as they should be. I do not claim that thej' are the best, but we are improving, we are going ahead. The Vancouver Sun of February 26 had this to say in regard to the propaganda my hon. friend is carrying on and its effect on British Columbia. The article is headed " Poor Publicity " and it goes on to say:
Hon. Harry Stevens, genial and able member for Vancouver Centre, tells his Ottawa confreres that high taxation, instituted by the Canadian government, is driving business men out of Vancouver into Seattle. Published broadcast in the east, this interesting statement has moved many eastern interests to inquire anxiously whether it is really true that the head offices 
of Vancouver firms are moving across the line. It is not true. In straining after ammunition wherewith to blast his political opponents, Mr. Stevens has this time somewhat overreached himself. Instead of devastating the Liberal forces, Mr. Stevens has simply managed to give his own constituency a black eye. Canadian taxation may be high. No one will deny that. But Mr. Stevens' support of the present freight rates discrimination against Vancouver and the remarkably poor publicity he gives this city in statements like this one will do more to drive Vancouver firms out of business than will our present taxation.
I think I may be permitted to follow that up and to show the progress that British Columbia is making in the industries in which she is directly interested. The lumber industry is one of our largest. Probably no other province in Canada has the stand of timber that British Columbia has, and in no province has the industry developed so rapidly as in British Columbia. I took occasion to write the Department of Lands in Victoria, B.C. asking them in regard to the increase in the lumber business over a period of years, and I propose to place these figures on Hansard. Before doing so, I purpose reading a letter from the minister of that department, because we hear in this House statements in regard to the administration of the lumber industry, not only in British Columbia, but in other provinces, and I think the minister's letter might well be placed on Hansard. He writes as follows:
February 25, 1925.
Hon. Dr. J. H. King. M.P.,
Minister of Public Works,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Dr. King,
In reply to your telegram of February 23. I enclose herewith memo showing export, as requested by you.
I may say the policy of the government is that manufacturing shall take place within the province. As hon. members are aware, we have no control over export of logs from crown granted areas. In the case of licenses, each case is dealt with on its merits and export is only allowed where there is no local market. On the other hand, no export would be allowed if operations were deliberately carried on for the purpose of glutting the market.
This is signed by the Minister of Lands in British Columbia.
I think I might fairly explain to the House the matter of export of logs from the province of British Columbia. We have large stands of timber there and in our logging operations we find that only certain grades of timber will be absorbed in our own or local markets: that is the lumberman or operator cannot saw a No. 3 or No. 4 grade log and expect to ship that class of timber with the freight rates that it carries into the prairie districts or into the foreign markets. So that in the logging operations we have what is known as a third and fourth grade of logs, which if made into lum-

The Budget-Mr. King (Kootenay)
ber, in thickly populated areas would be absorbed locally, but would not permit of sale if one had to export over a long rail or ocean trip. So that we have in British Columbia the exportation erf certain grades of logs, more particularly Nos. 3 and 4. These are only allowed to be exported on a certificate of officials of the department and by order in council of the government. Now as to the growth of the industry, I will just briefly state it. The following figures will show the water borne lumber trade, logs exported and the total scale of logs:

The mining industry is of great interest and great value to the people of British Columbia, and I think never in its history has it been in a more flourishing condition than it is at the present time. The value of our mineral products for 1924, according to a conservative estimate, will total $45,000,000. This is 9 per cent better than $41,000,000 in 1923. This does not tell the whole story for the year 1924 because during that year the coal mining operations within the province suffered very materially, more particularly in the Crowsnest pass district where a strike continuing over seven months lessened production by 750,000 tons. If we eliminate the coal mining, the metal mining wall show an increase of 25 per cent in 1924 over 1923. A few miles north of Vancouver we have one of the largest copper mines in the empire. This class of mining has not been over-prosperous on account of the weak markets due to the unsettled conditions that existed in Europe following the war; yet a comparison of the years 1922, 1923 and 1924 shows continuous progress in that industry. In 1922 we produced 32,359,000 pounds of copper; in 1923, 57,720,000 pounds, and in 1924, 63,185,000 pounds. It is true a great deal of this metal is shipped out of the -country in the raw state, but as I said this afternoon, the policy of the Liberal party in bonusing this mining industry has brought results. In the budget brought down some few years ago the
government gave a bonus for the production of refined copper in Canada, and within the last few months this bonus has had its effect. Copper is being refined at the Trail smelter in British Columbia to-day, and some 600 tons of that refined copper is now in eastern Canada and being manufactured into copper wares in this country. In addition to that we have the annual statement of the Consolidated Mining Company in which they say:
As expected the year's average prices of lead and zinc were favourable. In the latter part of the year the copper position improved. On the expectation that the market price of this metal will remain above 14 cents a pound for some time, preparations are being made to resume operations by the Allenby Copper Company at Copper Mountain, near Princeton, B.C
Capper Mountain has one of the largest deposits of copper in the world, but it has been closed down for a numlber of years, and to-day under the stimulus of the bonus and the increased price of copper, we have further assurance that this mine will be in operation this year. But, Mr. Speaker, probably the brightest phase in the mining industry in any country is the development of the lead and zinc industry in Britsh Columbia. The development of the Portland canal district, where is located the famous Premier mine, the mine carrying very high grade silver and producing great wealth, gives promise of great production, from other properties. I have referred, Mr. Speaker, at some length to the industrial activity in British Columbia, in order that I might dispel the picture of gloom and despair that has been painted by some of the hon. members opposite. Last night -my hon. friend from Comox-Aiberni, (Mr. Neill) dealt with the fishing industry in British Columbia and informed the House that the year 1924 was the best year ever enjoyed in the salmon fishery business since 1919. Agriculturists in the province have suffered, as agriculturists have suffered the world over, but I find that last year there was an improved feeling among them.
Now. as to taxation. A few days ago the hon. member for Vancouver Centre suggested that taxation to-day is stifling industry, and that this government is at fault in regard to it. No one will deny for a moment that taxes are high, and no sane or reasonable man will wonder why they are high. During the war period we expended large sums of money both at the front and at home, and to-day we are carrying the burden. We were told the other day by my hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) that probably we would be well advised to adopt the French policy and raise our tariffs - to a very high point, but he did not suggest that we should not pay our war debt; and I believe it was the intention of our people when they borrowed money to prosecute the 'war to repay it. So to-day we have high taxation. But as shown by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) $900,000,000 of our war loans are tax free, but as those loans mature and are refunded they will become taxable.
I have made some inquiries regarding taxation in this country and in the United States, and I have before me a comparison of the income tax on corporations as levied in the two countries. I am advised that in the United States this tax is 12J per cent, while ours is 10J per cent. These figures are given me by the Commissioner of Taxation and I have no doubt they are absolutely reliable. It is therefore apparent that Canadian corporations have an advantage over those in the States to the extent of 2 per cent in this respect. My hon. friends opposite these days seem to be very anxious to make comparisons between Canada and the United States in an attempt to show that we are very much worse off than our neighbours. But it is very difficult to make reliable comparisons, our federal and provincial jurisdictions being different to the federal and state jurisdictions across the line. Some of our provinces im-

pose income tax, and over this the federal government has no control, and because of this it may be that corporations in this country are paying more in income tax than corporations in the United States. I am not sure whether income tax is imposed by some of the states, but I know that the states adjoining British Columbia do not impose any.
My hon. friend from Vancouver Centre also invited the attention of the Acting Minister of Finance to the fact that non-residents in Great Britain or the United States who purchase goods for export are subject to tax. Well, a non-resident in Great Britain, the United States or Canada, who purchases goods for export only is not subject to income tax. My hon. friend also intimated that an outsider who might come in and do business in England would be presented by the tax commissioner or his agent with an assessment as representing a foreign firm. This statement implies that the Old Country imposes a tax on those who effect purchases therefrom, but I am advised that .this is not the case. Foreign companies transacting business in Great Britain through agents or representatives are taxable on profits realized within the United Kingdom, but not in respect to purchases for export only. Great Britain also assesses resident corporations, although they be foreign, where the actual control and management is within the United Kingdom. Preliminary operations in manufacture by foreign companies within Canada are deemed by statutory declaration to be the partial exercise of business or the carrying on of business in Canada, and consequently within the purview of the income tax law. The minister may determine, and his determination is final, what portion of the ultimate total profit made by the sale abroad of the semi-manufactured goods referred to should be taxed in Canada. So we find that a foreign firm with an agency in Vancouver is assessed at the discretion of the minister, and his word is final as to the profits made and the assessment thereon.
I have before me extracts from the Income War Tax Act which I should like to place on Hansard to save time, as I am anxious not to detain the House.

CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate, I first wish to congratulate the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on being able to bring down a budget that was mucn more acceptable to this House and to Canada than any of us had reason to expect. Of course we all realize that it would be absolutely impossible to bring down a budget that would be acceptable to everybody. We have in the eastern sections of Canada the manufacturers, who want high protection and we have the prairie provinces in the west, that want free trade. The farmers on the prairies have to compete in the markets of the world with what they produce, and naturally they think they should have the right to buy what they want where they can get it the cheapest. Then we have our large railway system, which the private companies failed to make a success of; a system which was in a very dilapidated condition when the government took it over-in fact it was not
The Budget-Mr. McBride

safe to run trains on several of the lines, at least at any speed. On the one hand we have the people talking day after day about cheap freight rates; on the other we have Sir Henry Thornton and his officers making every effort to get our railways on a paying basis. Then we have the Acting Finance Minister and the government trying to keep expenditure within revenue; on the other hand w'e have members of parliament, or at least a percentage of them, who want more expenditure and less taxation. Under these conditions I do not think it is possible for any man to bring down a budget that would be acceptable in all quarters of the House.
Since the House opened on February 5 a good deal has been said about hard times; about people going to the United States; about unemployment; about getting more immigrants into the country; about less taxation and greater expenditure; about ocean freight rates; about the merchant marine; about cheap money for the farmers and how to run the banks. Others have talked about Senate reform; some about a reduction of the indemnity; some about annexation to the United States. Indeed some people go around the country suggesting that this government is in favour of annexation, or words to that effect. My experience has been that a man with a pair of good sound lungs does not have to go round the country telling the people what he has got; no, they will perform the functions they were intended to perform, without any special effort on his part. As I see it, no true Canadian will go round the country making such a statement; only the skimmed milk type of politician would do such work.
\\ e have heard, as I have already said, a good deal about people going over to the United States. I might make the statement that 250,000 people came from the United States to Vancouver last year, and1 it would be just as correct, as some of the statements that have been made in this House. The statement is correct, but it is misleading and should not be made. They came over, but the greater number of them went back. Why run down Canada? Why have people so much to say about the United States? Why do they hold the United States up as a country of prosperity, a country to be desired by all, and why do they paint a gloomy and foreboding picture of their own country? There are two or three statements I would like to make in connection with our people going over to the United States. Here is a letter from a young man who went to California in 1923. He says:

I do not care much for California; I find it very hard to get acquainted. The people seem to think of nothing here but the almighty dollar, and I think every crook from hell to bedlam must be in California.
I have given it word for word as it was written. He says further:
The favourite sport seems to be trying how often you can get married and divorced in the same year. Stealing other men's wives is another way of passing the time, and robbing at the point of the gun is as common as swatting mosquitoes in the Smith meadows during the month of June.
We have heard a great deal about the condition of prosperity in the United States and the inducements that are offered to Canadians to go there, while at the same time a gloomy picture is painted of Canada. Here is what Sam Gompers, president of the American Federation of Labour for a great number of years in the United States, said on the 5th of November last-and I may say that on the 5th of November there were not a great number of people out of employment in Canada, in British Columbia at least:
All this talk of prosperity in the United States looks good on paper. We hear much about it, but right now we have at least two million people out of work.
That was on the 5th of November last year. Is that a very desirable country for our people to go to? Still another:	Mrs. J.
H. Bullman, president of the Illinois Federation of Women's Clubs, in an address before the leaders of that body in Chicago on December 12, makes this statement-these are not Canadians; they are Americans:
There should be more hanging and less sobbing over the plight of the youthful gunmen and ex-murderers and toughs.
Then she goes on to say:
We are the most lawless nation on the earth. Our criminal record is unequalled in any city on the globe. With such a condition why should we talk about abandoning capital punishment? Every five and a half years more lives were lost through crime than were lost in the war. I am tired of this silly sentimentality that favours the treatment of crime.
And she closed by urging that there be no cutting down of the number of hangings until crime is lessened. Yet the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) makes reference this afternoon to the "magnificent" country to the south of us. Glowing terms, siplendid words -about the country to the south; but what about Canada? He holds up poor old England and Canada as the picture of distress-as if they were not fit to take care of themselves. There was more unemployment-yes, five times more-in Vancouver in the spring of 1913 or 1914 than there has been since this government came into power.

The Budget-Mr. McBride
It has been stated by an hon. member of the opposition that the housing problem in this country is solving itself; that the people did not need any more houses, because they were leaving the country. Well, I do not know very much about Canada, but I know a little about a town out on the Pacific coast which they used to call Gastown; then they called it Vancouver, and1 now some people call it Greater Vancouver. I am going to say a little about what has been going on there. During the year 1924 there were 2,032 homes built in that city, and there is scarcely an empty house in it; indeed when I went back after the last session I had to call up a number of hotels before I was able to get a room. Here is what the building inspector says:
On December 31st when the building inspectors of the various districts which make up Greater Vancouver compiled their figures for the year 1924, they stated it was one of the greatest years of construction in the history of the lower mainland. The total value of buildings erected was 112,882,474, an increase of 90 per cent over the previous year.
Does that look as if people were leaving this country or had lost confidence in it? But that is not all:
On December 31st, there was under construction, proceeding or contracted, an additional nine millions, or a grand total of twenty-two millions for the year 1924.
I think that is a record this country should be proud of. It is a record the people should know about, and it is one that will do much to counteract the attempt being made to becloud the issue all over this country. I do not know that I will say much more about Vancouver. I do not wish to make one of those long-winded speeches lasting two or three hours. I will pass on.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) last night dealt fully with the oriental question. Indeed, many of the items that he had in his address I intended to bring before this House. However, I do not intend to repeat what he has already said, and said so well, and I will be as brief as possible. I will give you a quotation from a Japanese paper translated into the English language. This publication says:
There is danger ahead. Discrimination has been shown in the school question, which is extremely important, and in the fishing question. We Japanese to whom it is a question of life and death struggle must determine it at any sacrifice.
That is what the Japanese say themselves in their own paper. Indeed, if the Japanese did not stand by their country in case of trouble, they would be executed for treason by their own countrymen. That is the opinion of a 116
judge of the Supreme court of British Columbia, and I quite agree with him. Why should1 we be bringing in orientals to Canada and educating them in our schools at the expense of the taxpayers of this country, when we cannot furnish money to educate our own children? Why should these people be coming to this country to take the place of our own men in business? We have got to educate them for the purpose, and then allow them to enter business to compete with the white race. Why should we in British Columbia be compelled by this government to allow those people to come to this country, and have them sit in the same schools with our white boys and girls? I have nothing to say against the oriental idea of morals; that is their own business, not ours. But I do say that this government should stop, and stop once for all, those people coming in and placing themselves alongside our children in the schools, where our children will have a chance to talk with them. It is all very good for people down here who do not know, but it is a serious question out in British Columbia, and I think this government should realize it, and the sooner they do, the better it will be for all concerned.
We hear a great deal about the Japanese high temperament, and the position they will take if we say thiat this country does not want to have them here. If the Japanese had any self-respect, shall I say, they would not come to Canada, for well they know they are not wanted. They are forcing themselves in on us. Would any self-respecting people do that? I do not think they would. And when you bring the oriental race and the white race together, what do you have? In the first case, they will not assimilate, but they are getting married, and they are bringing into existence a mongrel race that is not a credit to any country. It is certainly not a credit to Canada, and should not be allowed. In fact if this parliament is going to allow these people to come in here it ought to do as the States have done, make a law forbidding orientals and the white race to unite in marriage, and the sooner that is done, the better it will be for all concerned.
We have out there in British Columbia over forty thousand of these orientals, and last year there were about twelve hundred births. Surely that is enough of 9 p.m. increase without allowing any more orientals to come to our shores. Not only that, the Japanese themselves take objection to cheap labour. I read this in a Japanese paper:



The Budget-Mr. McBride
The Tokio government fears cheap labour from China. Drastic action which may result in the deportation of 6,000 Chinese labouring now in Japan is expected from the Japanese government. Chinese labour is affecting employment in Japan, as the Chinese work for smaller wages.
Now if Japan claims the right to deport labour that they bring in when they have finished their work, surely Canada has that right too. Why should she not have this right? Even India has taken the stand to keep outsiders from coming into her country. I read this from Delhi, India:
A bill was passed for the purpose of regulating the entry into British India of persons who were domiciled in other British possessions.
The British representative on the executive council did not oppose that bill. Now if India can regulate her immigration, why cannot Canada? I have another item here from Capetown, South Africa, The Transvaal and Free State:
Asiatic segregation contemplated by South Africa, also Belgrade. The Jugo-Slav Minister of Commerce has published a decree requesting all foreigners to leave. Friendly nations are granted a short delay not to exceed four weeks.
Is this not evidence enough that Canada should have the right to regulate her immigration? Not only that, but there is no Class of people in British Columbia to-day that has as much tuberculosis as the orientals have. That has been proven by statistics. And these orientals are in the market gardening business. They are supplying vegetables [DOT]to the hotels and restaurants and to many private houses. Now is it right that that class of people should1 be handling vegetables and spreading that disease that is costing British Columbia to-day and other countries thousands, yes, millions of dollars to try and stamp it out? Yet that is what is going on. Indeed, there was a case of leprosy a short [DOT]time ago in British Columbia, and1 this man was also engaged in market gardening, with every opportunity to spread the disease. We have quite enough people of our own to run this country, and when the good Lord made the orientals and the white race he put the Pacific ocean between them to keep them apart.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The white men were here before the orientals, and the orientals are not pioneers. They do not go out to help develop the country, never have and never will. They always stay around the cities. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill)

spoke last evening on the subject of naval defence. I should like to say a word or two on the same question. It seems to me this government should do something to give us protection on the Pacific coast. I am not advocating a standing army for Canada. The only necessity for such an army as I see it, would be in the event of trouble between us and our friends to the south-something that nobody ever expects to see, it is quite unthinkable. I do not think Canada should spend money on a standing army but I do believe that adequate provision should be made so as to protect our shores and our ports in case of trouble. Also to enable us to remain neutral, if we wanted to do so, in the event of a clash between other countries. Supposing, for instance trouble arose between United States and Japan and a naval battle occurred between the ships of those countries off the Pacific coast? Supposing the Japanese fleet got the worst of it where would they head for? They would make either for Prince Rupert or Esquimalt, possibly for Vancouver. We may as well realize it the Japanese fleet could enter Prince Rupert, or the harbours of Esquimalt, Victoria or Vancouver and command these cities to surrender. We could not defend ourselves; we have nothing to defend ourselves with. And supposing the Japanese fleet entered Vancouver harbour? Under international law Canada might permit them to remain for twenty-four hours but no longer. At the expiration of that time this country would have to force the evacuation of that harbour or run the risk of bombardment by the United States navy. How could we force the Japanese to withdraw, if they did not wish to go, seeing that we have no means of compelling them. We should simply, in the absence of an adequate force of our own, have to let the Americans come in, and that would be a very humiliating position to be placed in. Then if the Japanese showed fight the Americans would have to bombard their fleet in the harbour and possibly blow up our towns and our docks. It is a serious proposition for us on the Pacific coast. Other countries are preparing for eventualities of this kind and why-should not Canada. Sometimes we hear people talking about Canada being in no danger, that the United States and Britain would afford the necessary protection in such case of an emergency. It reminds me of the man who had three sons. He set them up in business but when they got into financial difficulties they always came to talk it over with the old man and to get him to foot the bill. That is not a very dignified procedure,

The Budget-Mr. McBride
but it is just what Canada would have to do in the event of such hostilities as I have alluded to breaking out because she could not protect herself. We must look at the facts as they are and not as we would wish them to be. The experience of other countries ought to be valuable to us in a matter of this kind; it is a far safer guide than theory. The experience of England is particularly useful. It has shown that it takes three years to build a warship, and nine years to train a crew. If we trust to civilization there is no guarantee of security. Only the nation that can protect itself is in a position to rest in safety.
Now, what is the United States doing? I am not going to enter upon a consideration of the entire programme of the United States for defence purposes. I shall cite only one instance. In 1924 the number of guns mounted for the defence of Panama was as follows:
Pacific Coast-
One 16" gun range 50,000 yards.
Six 14" guns.
Fourteen 6" guns.
Twelve 12" howitzers.
Twelve 4.7" howitzers.
On the Atlantic coast the artillery mounted for the same purpose is as follows:
Atlantic coast-
Four 14" guns.
Four 12" , guns.
Six 6" guns.
Sixteen 12" howitzers.
Eight 4.7" howitzers.
Sixty-six 3" guns.
In addition there is a mobile armament consisting of fifty-two, 155mm. guns, tractor drawn. This year the United States is budgeting for the following additions to the defence of Panama:
Four 16'' guns for the Pacific at a cost of $1,200,000.
Four 16'' guns for the Atlantic at a cost of $1,060,000.
Surely if the country to the south is impressed with the necessity of making such preparations we ought to do something to protect our part of the Pacific coast. It is possible that Canada could impose on the generosity of the British government in order to protect herself on the Atlantic should trouble break out there but we could not do that on the Pacific; we are too far away. The Dominion of New Zealand last year voted $5,000,000 for this purpose; a little country like New Zealand. We claim that the Canadian people are going to be a great nation in a short time and therefore why should we not make some preparations to defend ourselves? I think it should be the duty of this government to at least make a start this session in providing 116i
some protection for the Pacific coast. They are in honour bound to do it.
Now I come to a consideration of railway matters. We have not heard very much on this subject this session but I hope to hear the question discussed before the session is over. I should like to refer for a few minutes to the matter of an outlet to the Peace river country. I am not going to labour the question, I am not going to ask hon. members to take any statements of mine; I will give you statements taken from a report published in 1920 and signed by Hon. Arthur Meighen and W. W. Cory, Deputy Minister of the Interior. I went up into that country and spent part of a fall there before I ever mentioned the subject here-I wanted to be sure that I could verify any statements I intended to make and I will now say that I have no fault to find with that report as a whole. I will just give you a few extracts from the report in order to show you what the country is like:
First, the area of the Peace River district is over 115,000 square miles. Three and a half million acres of the best of this land is owned by the Dominion government.
The climate of the Peace River district is excellent. Blizzards are unknown. Seeding usually begins early in April, sometimes in March. Most of the rainfalls occur in June and July. Mild weather until Christmas is not uncommon.
In 1919 there were shipped out over the Edmonton and Dunvegan railway, 4,909 carloads of freight. In the same year there were shipped in 4,143 carloads of freight. Marquis wheat has yielded as high as 69 bushels to the acre.
Now as to Pouce Coupe:
The extent of this choice area is about 25 miles wide by 40 miles long. The altitude is low. Summer frost and hail are very rare, and total crop failure from any cause is unknown.
The mountain streams contain trout. Cariboo lake teems with large trout and white fish.
Seams of coal are exposed in the canyon above Hudson Hope. Beds of gypsum ten to fifteen feet are exposed on both banks of the Peace river for a distance of fifteen miles.
As regards coal there is practically no limit to the coal areas there and to the available water-power. People went into that district believing the federal government were going to provide railway transportation for them. A circular to that effect was distributed all over the United States and the Old Country, and settlers went in there confident that the government were going to provide them with transportation. As to the kind of people in the Peace river country I am prepared to say I never encountered a better class anywhere. They are the pioneer type. They are men and women who are willing to make good and who will make good if they get half a chance. Why will this government not do something
The Budget-Mr. McBride

to give them an outlet? I know the finances of this country will not permit very large expenditures on railways, and I am not asking for that. I should like to see an outlet by way of Prince George, but I understand that would cost in the neighbourhood of $17,000,000, and I am not asking even for that at the present time. What I would like this government to do-and the outlay would be only a small one-is to see to it that the piece of line between Spirit river and Pouce Coupe, fifty-four miles long, which is already graded and which is practically ready to lay the steel on, is completed and to extend it ten miles further into the Peace river block. This would make, all told, sixty-four miles. Surely that would not 'be a big thing. When the line is built, I would like to see the government turn it over to whatever railway is operating the Edmonton-Dunvegan line on condition that they would reduce the freight rates that now exist from the Peace river block to Edmonton. They could then leave the country alone for a few years to see whether it would develop as fast as a large number of us who know the district think it would. I think that would satisfy the people there, and for the present it would give them an outlet. I believe it would serve the purpose; the expenditure would be very small, and it would redeem the pledges given by the federal government to the people who went in there. I think the government would be fully justified in carrying out this project.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Did the hon. member
see the press report recently ito the effect that the Canadian Pacific are negotiating with the government at the moment whereby they are to be given a subsidy of some $180,000 to bring the Peace river grain out over the British Columbia and Edmomton-Dunvegan line?

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have seen that report
in the newspapers. Further than that, I know nothing of it; but even if that were done, it would not give the people in the Peace river block any accommodation in the way of railway facilities. That would be only to operate the lines that are already there, that is, in Alberta. I think the government is in honour bound to carry out this extension, and I think the people would back them in doing so. As I have already said, this would be only fair to the people who are in there.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Approximately, how many
people are in there ?

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would not say how many are in there at the present time. I do not think in the Peace river block there would be possibly more than two thousand. I was told that at one time there were between seven and eight thousand but I will say this, that when I was through that country, I met only one man who wanted to sell his place. They have their patents on their homesteads and they are keeping them until they get railway facilities while they are living in other places. You can readily understand why people are leaving that district. I have seen men who had built three granaries. They build first one granary, then an addition and then another addition, each year for three years, to hold the grain waiting for railway facilities. In other places, they have two and three years' grain stacked in the fields. They grow the grain because they like to grow it, and they are trying to live there as best they can. It is a general thing for the men to go to Vancouver or the United States, wherever they can get a job, in the winter time, leaving their wives and families to look after the cattle, while they earn a little money with which to buy the necessaries of life. Yet they have the grain there if they could get it to market. Why not give them an outlet?
A good deal has been said about immigration into Canada, and I expect a good deal more will be said. I do not think Canada will ever ibe right until we have thirty or forty million people. At the same time, I cannot say that I am in favour of this government taxing the people of Canada to bring a certain class of people to this country. I come from the Old Country, and I have never seen the time there that a man, if he wanted to earn his passage to Canada, could not do so in less than two years. If a man has not backbone enough to earn his passage out here, what is he going to do when he gets here? Such men are going to flock into the cities or come and whine to the government to lend them money or something along that line. Let me give an instance. Last spring, two young men who received assisted passages to Canada came out to British Columbia and went to work on a farm that I am very well acquainted with. They said they were raised on a farm in the Old Country; that they had worked on a farm all their lives. One of them worked for about four and a half months and the other, for about five and a half months. I know the man for whom they were working gave them every opportunity. At the end of that time neither one of them could hitch up a team, take it out and do a day's ploughing.

The Budget-Mr. McBride
That was not the worst of the matter. The farmer had finally to pay them off, and neither of the men had ten dollars saved when he paid them; they were always borrowing money ahead. When they were asked what they would do for the winter, they said they thought they would go to Vancouver, that the people there would not let them starve. Such people are no good and they are a curse to the workingmen of the country. They go to the cities, take whatever jobs they can get, at any wage, and put the working men out of their steady jobs. We do not want that class in Canada. Any man who wants to make good can earn enough to bring him to this country, and if he cannot do that we do not want him here.
A good deal has been said from all parts of this House about the tariff, and as far as I can see, it makes very' little difference whether the tariff is high or low as long as the government will see to it that the manufacturers in Canada will produce goods just as cheap as we can buy them on the American side. That is all we ask. That is all the farmer asks. Why should the farmers of this country, who have to compete in the markets of the world, foe put up against a tariff of 25 or 35 per cent when they go to buy anything? That is not right. Some people say that Canada cannot compete with the United States. Canada can compete with the United States. She can give the United States cards and spades and beat them to it. The young men of Canada proved the stuff they were made of when they went to France and Flanders and they can do so again. The trouble with our manufacturers is that they are too mean to purchase up-to-date machinery and give our young men a chance to make good. If they were given to understand that they would get protection provided they put their goods on the market as cheap as they could be purchased on the other side, but that if they commenced to hold the people up in this country, the tariff would be cut down, that would have the desired effect, and I think it is what ought to be done.
I had a letter from British Columbia the other day, in connection with eggs and butter. I think the government during the present session should raise the dtuty on eggs coming into Canada to make it equal to the duty on the same article going into the States. There is nothing wrong about that and I think it is only fair. Some members laugh at that; the trouble is that protection is not for the farmer. He gets no
protection, and the manufacturer is protected all the time. Now a certain class of people start in a small way. They take up a homestead; they have a cow and a few chickens and try to make a living in that way. Why should they not be given the same protection as the manufacturers? Why should the government not put a duty of 8 cents a dozen on eggs, as the United States does? Why should they not also put a duty on butter?
I should like to say a word in connection with the farmers being given this rural credit that has been spoken of. Anything I may say has no reference to returned men whatever. In my view neither this government nor the provincial government can do too much for the returned men-the men who did so much for Canada-but I am absolutely opposed to this government starting to give credit to farmers or anyone else. Let the provincial government look after that. I have heard the provincial government out in British Columbia boasting that they could borrow money cheaper than the Dominion government. Why then should the Dominion government get mixed up in this proposition? Why should they place a blanket mortgage on British Columbia or on Quebec or any other province, in order to be able to give the farmers cheap money? That is exactly what they have been doing. If Mr. Brown has his farm clear of mortgage, why should this government place a mortgage on that farm in order to be able to lend me cheap money? It is not a good policy, and if this government wants to get into trouble, it seems to me that would be a good way to go about it.
In conclusion I have a few words to say about railway rates. We 'have heard a great deal about railway rates and about putting our railways on a paying basis. Some farmers say, "Reduce the rates and carry more grain." What would the farmers say if the railways said, "Produce more grain, and lower your price for grain, and you will make more money"? The one is just as good an argument as the other. In my opinion it is up to this government to increase the rates from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Some people say that if you increased rates on the Canadian National you would drive all the traffic to the Canadian Pacific. Well, increase the rates on the Canadian Pacific also. As I view the matter, I think it would be a simple thing for this government to increase the rates on *both lines, say 10 per cent; then tax both lines 90 per cent of that 10 per cent and you
The Budget-Mr. McBride

will get a revenue that will carry our railways and finance the country. I think that is a reasonable .proposition. They would not then be making any moTe profit on the Canadian Pacific railway than 'they are making at present, or very 'little more. Canada will never be as prosperous as she should be until our railways are on a paying basis. I say further that districts which have no railway connection should not be 'taxed to give cheaper freight rates to those districts which have connections with the main lines. Take for instance a firm that I am very well acquainted1 with in British Columbia which got in nine carloads of freight last month. There is not one member of this House who did not help to .pay the freight rates on those nine cars. W'hy should they? The people who are making the profit are the people who should pay. At present every member in this House is helping to pay for the freight on those cars, because the National railway is carrying 'them for less than cost. I do not see that it is reasonable that we should put Sir Henry Thornton and his men u,p against an impossible proposition. I have no hesitation in saying that Sir Henry Thornton and Ws staff are doing everything that it is possible for them to do to give a good service to Canada and1 to place the railways on a paying basis. But they cannot do it. It is an absolute impossibility at the present rates. If the freight rates were increased, they would not be any higher than they are in the United' States. I have a schedule here showing the rates on one side of the line and the rates on the other side of the line, and I find that where they are carrying wheat, for instance, at 22 cents a bushel on the Canadian side they are charging 37 cents on the American side, and I find in another instance where they are carrying wheat for 20 cents on the Canadian side .they are charging 35 cents on the American side. According to this schedule the rates are fifteen to twenty per cent higher on the American side than on the Canadian side.
